_note: Tide DESTINATION pages: recognizable coastal places people search for ('Cannon Beach tides') that don't have their own NOAA station. Each maps to its nearest source station (by slug, from tide-stations.mjs); the destination page shows that station's predictions and states the distance honestly. Distance is computed at build time from the coords below, so only the mapping + coords need to be right. Proof-of-concept: Oregon. Expand by state, prioritized by Search Console impressions.

destinations.name: Seaside
destinations.blurb: Oregon's classic beach resort town, with a mile-and-a-half oceanfront Promenade and a wide, flat beach where the water sweeps a long way in and out across the sand.

destinations.name: Cannon Beach
destinations.blurb: Home to Haystack Rock, one of the most photographed sea stacks on the Pacific coast. Its tide pools sit at the base of the rock and are only reachable around low tide, so the day's low is what matters here.

destinations.name: Rockaway Beach
destinations.blurb: A seven-mile stretch of open sand on the north Oregon coast, popular for beachcombing and known for the Twin Rocks landmark standing just offshore.

destinations.name: Pacific City
destinations.blurb: Known for its own Haystack Rock and the flat-bottomed dory boats that launch straight off the beach through the surf — both the launch and the landing depend on the tide.

destinations.name: Lincoln City
destinations.blurb: More than seven miles of open beach on the central coast, famous for the hand-blown glass floats hidden along the sand and for its wide flats at low tide.

destinations.name: Depoe Bay
destinations.blurb: Billed as the world's smallest navigable harbor and a well-known whale-watching spot; the narrow channel and the tide-driven spouting horns make the water level here worth checking.

destinations.name: Waldport
destinations.blurb: A quiet town at the mouth of Alsea Bay, where the estuary's tide flats draw clammers and crabbers when the water pulls back.

destinations.name: Yachats
destinations.blurb: A small village where the Yachats River meets the sea over a rocky shore; the tide pools and spouting rocks are best explored near low water.

destinations.name: Bandon
destinations.blurb: Known for Face Rock and a shoreline studded with sea stacks; the beach and its tide pools open up as the tide drops.

destinations.name: Coos Bay
destinations.blurb: The largest city on the Oregon coast, set on a working estuary where the tide governs the bay's channels and mudflats.

destinations.name: Sausalito
destinations.blurb: A small, hilly waterfront town on San Francisco Bay's Marin shore, known for its houseboat community and calm harbor just across the Golden Gate from the city.

destinations.name: Tiburon
destinations.blurb: A quiet peninsula town on San Francisco Bay, popular for its waterfront paths and ferry views; the bay's tides set the pace along its shoreline.

destinations.name: Pacifica
destinations.blurb: A string of open Pacific beaches just south of San Francisco, popular with surfers and tide-pool hunters when the water pulls back.

destinations.name: Half Moon Bay
destinations.blurb: A coastal town known for its long state beaches and the big-wave break at nearby Mavericks; low tide opens up wide stretches of sand.

destinations.name: Santa Cruz
destinations.blurb: Home to a famous beach boardwalk and surf breaks on the north shore of Monterey Bay; the tide pools along West Cliff are best at low water.

destinations.name: Capitola
destinations.blurb: A small, colorful beach village on Monterey Bay just east of Santa Cruz, with a compact beach that narrows at high tide.

destinations.name: Malibu
destinations.blurb: A long ribbon of Southern California beaches and points; several coves and tide pools here are only reachable around low tide.

destinations.name: Huntington Beach
destinations.blurb: Known as Surf City, with miles of wide, flat sand where the surf and the tide shape the day's conditions.

destinations.name: Long Beach
destinations.blurb: A long stretch of flat, drivable sand on the Long Beach Peninsula — one of the longest beaches in the country, with big swings across the shallow flats.

destinations.name: Ocean Shores
destinations.blurb: A resort town at the mouth of Grays Harbor, with broad sandy beaches and interior canals; the tide fills the flats quickly here.

destinations.name: Edmonds
destinations.blurb: A small ferry town on Puget Sound just north of Seattle, with a waterfront and beach where the Sound's large tides expose wide flats.

destinations.name: Des Moines
destinations.blurb: A marina town on Puget Sound south of Seattle, with a public beach and fishing pier where Puget Sound's tides run large.

destinations.name: Sarasota
destinations.blurb: A Gulf Coast city known for its barrier-island beaches and calm bay; Gulf tides here are gentle, usually just a foot or two.

destinations.name: Siesta Key
destinations.blurb: A barrier island off Sarasota famous for its powdery quartz-sand beach; the Gulf's small tides make for wide, easy-walking sand.

destinations.name: Fort Lauderdale
destinations.blurb: A Southeast Florida beach city laced with canals and waterways; the Atlantic tides here run a modest few feet, twice a day.

destinations.name: Destin
destinations.blurb: An Emerald Coast beach town on the Florida panhandle, known for white sand and clear water; the Gulf's tides here are small and often just one high a day.

destinations.name: South Padre Island
destinations.blurb: A barrier-island resort at Texas's southern tip, with wide Gulf beaches; both the Gulf and the Laguna Madre side see the small, often once-daily Gulf tide.

destinations.name: Port Aransas
destinations.blurb: A beach town on Mustang Island near Corpus Christi, popular for fishing and drivable beaches; the Gulf tides here are gentle and largely once-daily.

destinations.name: Cocoa Beach
destinations.blurb: A classic Space Coast surf town just south of Cape Canaveral, with a long, shallow-sloping Atlantic beach and the landmark Cocoa Beach Pier.

destinations.name: Daytona Beach
destinations.blurb: Home of the hard-packed "World's Most Famous Beach," where the wide Atlantic shoreline firms up enough to drive on near low tide.

destinations.name: Gulf Shores
destinations.blurb: Alabama's main Gulf Coast resort, with sugar-white sand and the small, slow, once-a-day tides typical of the northern Gulf of Mexico.

destinations.name: Tybee Island
destinations.blurb: Savannah's beach — a barrier island at the mouth of the Savannah River that shares the big semidiurnal tides of the Georgia coast.

destinations.name: Hilton Head Island
destinations.blurb: A Lowcountry resort island of wide, flat beaches where the water sweeps far out at low tide across hard-packed sand.

destinations.name: Nags Head
destinations.blurb: A central Outer Banks town on a narrow barrier island, with open Atlantic surf and the moderate tides of the North Carolina coast.

destinations.name: Ocean City
destinations.blurb: A family boardwalk resort on a South Jersey barrier island just below Atlantic City, on the mid-Atlantic's moderate tides.

destinations.name: Wildwood
destinations.blurb: Known for its exceptionally wide free beaches and neon "Doo-Wop" boardwalk at the southern tip of the New Jersey shore.

destinations.name: Rehoboth Beach
destinations.blurb: Delaware's flagship Atlantic beach town, with a mile-long boardwalk just down the coast from the Lewes tide station.

destinations.name: Laguna Beach
destinations.blurb: An Orange County cove-and-headland town famous for the tide pools that emerge at low tide along its rocky coves.

destinations.name: Oceanside
destinations.blurb: A North San Diego County surf city with a long sandy beach and a historic wooden pier, on Southern California's mixed tides.

destinations.name: Carmel-by-the-Sea
destinations.blurb: A storybook village beside a white-sand crescent bay on the Monterey Peninsula, on the mixed tides of the central California coast.

destinations.name: Pismo Beach
destinations.blurb: A wide, flat Central Coast beach known for clamming and dune riding, where low tide exposes a broad stretch of hard sand.

destinations.name: Morro Bay
destinations.blurb: A Central Coast town on a protected bay behind the landmark Morro Rock, with an estuary and harbor on mixed California tides.
